description:
Our chosen challenge is Space Mission Design Game, where we aim to develop an engaging, interactive simulation that combines realistic spaceflight physics, spacecraft design and strategic mission planning.

We are looking for enthusiastic team members with skills or interests in programming, game development, physics, UI/UX design, 3D modelling, graphic design and space science. However, anyone with creativity, enthusiasm and a willingness to contribute is welcome!
summary:
Perilune is an interactive 2D space mission design and simulation game developed in Rust. It allows players to explore the challenges of space exploration through spacecraft construction, mission planning, orbital mechanics and simulated spaceflight.

The project combines accessible gameplay with physics-based simulation, using scientific data and physical constants from NASA and JPL to model gravitational interactions and spacecraft movement. Players can experiment with different spacecraft designs, explore orbital trajectories and better understand the engineering decisions involved in planning space missions.

Perilune addresses the challenge by transforming complex concepts in aerospace engineering and orbital mechanics into an interactive educational experience. Rather than simply presenting information about space exploration, it encourages players to learn through experimentation, problem-solving and the consequences of their design decisions.

The project aims to make space mission design more accessible and engaging, particularly for students and anyone interested in physics, engineering and space exploration. By combining scientific principles with interactive gameplay, this project demonstrates how simulation can support STEM education and inspire greater interest in space science.
details:
Project Details - Perilune

Perilune is a 2D space mission design and simulation game that we developed using Rust. The aim of the project was to create something that makes space exploration and the science behind it more accessible, while still being enjoyable to play. Rather than simply reading about orbital mechanics or spacecraft engineering, players can experiment with these concepts themselves and see how their decisions affect a mission.

How the Game Works

Players can design their own spacecraft, experiment with different configurations and attempt missions using physics-based movement. The simulation takes into account gravitational forces and the movement of celestial bodies, allowing players to explore some of the challenges involved in real spaceflight.

One of our main priorities was finding a balance between realism and accessibility. We wanted the physics to be based on real scientific principles without making the game unnecessarily complicated for people who might not have much experience with space exploration.

Using NASA Data

NASA data plays an important role in Perilune. We used gravitational parameters and planetary measurements from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) to help model Earth, the Moon and their gravitational interactions.

We also incorporated NASA's lunar ephemeris data, which provides information about the Moon's position and orientation on specific dates. Other resources include research into the lunar south pole, particularly the Malapert region and Shackleton crater, where factors such as sunlight availability and communication are important considerations for future missions.

Another feature uses findings from NASA's LCROSS mission, which investigated the presence of water near the Moon's south pole. This allows players to explore some of the scientific research that contributes to real mission planning.

Although the game uses genuine NASA measurements, some aspects of the simulation have been simplified. For example, certain orbital models assume circular orbits, and celestial bodies are represented as spheres. These decisions helped make the simulation more manageable while retaining the scientific principles we wanted to demonstrate.

Development

We developed Perilune using the Rust programming language.

The application is available as a Windows executable, meaning it can be launched without needing to install Rust or a separate development environment. The scientific datasets are also stored locally, allowing the application to function offline.

All of the game's visuals, including the spacecraft, planets and interface elements, were created specifically for Perilune using geometric shapes and programmatically generated graphics.

Creativity and Challenges

One of the biggest challenges was combining several different aspects of space exploration into a single application. Spacecraft construction, orbital mechanics and scientific mission planning are all fairly complex subjects individually, so bringing them together while keeping the game understandable required careful consideration.

We also had to decide where scientific accuracy was most important and where simplifications would improve the experience. Our intention wasn't to create a perfect recreation of real spaceflight, but rather a game that demonstrates the underlying principles in an interesting and interactive way.

We think one of Perilune's more interesting features is how it brings together spacecraft engineering and actual NASA research. Players aren't just experimenting with rockets; they can also explore some of the scientific questions and challenges that influence real space missions.

Intended Impact

Ultimately, we hope Perilune encourages more people to take an interest in space exploration, physics and engineering. We believe interactive simulations can be an effective way of learning because they allow people to experiment, make mistakes and understand why something works rather than simply memorising information.

By combining gameplay with real NASA data, we wanted to show how scientific research can be used to create something both educational and entertaining, while giving players a better understanding of the challenges involved in exploring space.
